prize_parts.citation: for the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, based on reversible-terminator nucleotide chemistry on clustered single-molecule templates

statement.case_for: I keep B017 as my single preferred part and I now narrow it to Balasubramanian and Klenerman. The scientific case is unchanged and, after the full exchange, stronger: five of eight round-1 files name it, the principle is clear (nucleotide chemistry engineered into a parallel digital readout through reversible terminators, fluorescent labels and surface-clustered templates), it has been reproduced on independent platforms for two decades, and it opened capabilities in genomics and diagnostics that nobody had before. No member has argued it is immature. The Cambridge pair conceived and carried through the integrated chemistry, which is the discovery I would want a citation to name. Maturity and generative consequence both pass my test, and a two-name award is the version I can defend to a broad audience without having to adjudicate a priority dispute I cannot resolve from this record.
statement.case_against: The weakness is attribution, and narrowing to two names does not remove it: Rothberg (pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing), Ju (terminator chemistry) and Mayer (clonal colony amplification) all have real claims, and the 454 route is left outside the citation. Some will also read this as a scale-up of the sequencing recognised in 1980 and as a tool for biology and medicine more than a chemical discovery. I answer the last point with the content of the citation, which must name the chemistry of the reaction cycle and not the instrument or the downstream medicine. I accept that the exclusions remain a visible cost of a three-person cap on a field with five credible names.

responses.point: Aili would accept Mayer only if expert reports show the cluster idea was decisive, and otherwise prefers the clean Cambridge pair with a citation naming reversible terminators and clusters.
responses.response: I have moved towards her position. In round 1 I argued that clonal clustering is what makes the readout massively parallel and is separable from the terminator chemistry. I still think that is the right physical reading, but nothing in the material available to us tests Mayer's priority and experimental contribution against what Cambridge and Solexa built, and her condition is therefore not met. A chair should not put a third name into a citation on an argument that the committee cannot verify. I keep her wording about terminators and clusters in the citation, because it states the discovery in chemical terms and meets the question of whether this is chemistry.

responses.point: Aqvist keeps Mayer as the third laureate, but names the Cambridge pair alone as the cleaner option if no defensible third name can be agreed, and falls back to B048 only on cleanliness of attribution.
responses.response: His own fallback is the configuration I now propose, so I think we agree on the substance and differ on burden of proof. My question to him in round 1 was what evidence places Mayer's priority above Ju or Rothberg, and his statement says that his claims rest on background knowledge and are not verified. That is an honest answer, but it is not enough to justify a name in a public citation. I also disagree that B048 is the natural fallback if B017 is in difficulty: the attribution there is cleaner, but it is the same logic as the 2010 prize, and it should not take precedence over a discovery with a decidedly stronger generative case merely because the names are easier.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes a two-part prize: the Cambridge pair for B017 plus Rees alone for nitrogenase structure (B003).
responses.response: I agree with his reading of B017 and the attribution, which is now the same as mine. I do not support adding B003. He acknowledges himself that a Rees-only citation leaves out Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe, that the mechanism is still debated, and that the two parts have no joint motivation. A second part that needs a three-name expansion to be fair and a one-name restriction to fit the cap is not a defensible compromise. I also do not see a physical or chemical principle that links nitrogenase structure to sequencing, and a prize that has to be explained to a broad audience is stronger as one clear discovery. If the committee wants nitrogenase it should do so in a later year with the full set of contributors.

responses.point: Somfai prefers B048 (Buchwald and Hartwig) for its clean two-person attribution and argues that C-N coupling is a distinct catalyst-design problem from the 2010 C-C coupling prize, listing B017 as an alternative.
responses.response: His answer to my round-1 question is persuasive in part: C-N bond formation has its own catalyst-design logic, with ligand control of amine binding and reductive elimination, and I withdraw the implication that it is just a better ligand set. It remains in my alternatives. What keeps B017 ahead for me is the nature of the new capability: B048 improves how chemists make a bond they already made, in a field recognised in 2010, whereas sequencing by synthesis made an entirely new readout possible for nearly all of biology. He is right that Kosugi's tin-amide precedent needs wording, and that is a cost that B017 does not have in the same form.

responses.point: Zou keeps B041 first but calls it an accumulated field, notes it earned only one first place, and says B017 has far broader support and cleaner evidence of impact; his uncertainty is whether the Ju and Rothberg claims make a Cambridge-centred prize indefensible.
responses.response: I appreciate that he recognises B041 is a minority view and states that his proximity to the field may inflate it. On his question, I do not think that Ju and Rothberg make a Cambridge-centred award indefensible. Ju's terminator chemistry and Rothberg's pyrosequencing are alternative routes, whereas the Solexa chemistry is the one that became the dominant massively parallel platform, and a citation that is explicit about reversible terminators on clustered templates credits what was done without claiming that no other route existed. I concede that the 454 lineage is excluded by that wording and I regard this as a real cost, but that cost applies equally to every cut of three.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that excluding Mayer, Ju and Rothberg is defensible, since I cannot verify the detailed priority and patent history from the shortlist.
Whether the citation wording can credit reversible-terminator sequencing by synthesis without appearing to dismiss the pyrosequencing and semiconductor routes.
Whether members who did not rank B017 highly (Somfai, Sparr, Zou) see it as a viable prize part or as a tool for biology rather than a chemical discovery, and how that translates into votes.
Whether B048 is a stronger configuration than B017 if the committee puts weight on clean attribution over generative impact.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict. None of the shortlisted candidates is at Lund or in NanoLund, and my own work on thermoelectrics, ratchets and molecular motors does not overlap with any shortlisted discovery. Colleagueship with Somfai and Sparr at Lund is disclosed as not a conflict, and no member has reported a recusal.
